entries.1a7dcc3a489f24be7176dd16d710afb49eee03f5: Jdg 18:22-23 <div eID="gen3474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3475" type="x-p"/> The two clauses of Jdg 18:22 are circumstantial clauses: “<hi type="italic">When they</hi> (the 600) <hi type="italic">had got to some distance from Micah’s house, and the men who were in the houses by Micah’s house were called together, and had overtaken the Danites, they</hi> (i.e., Micah and his people, whom he had called together from the neighbourhood to pursue the emigrants) <hi type="italic">called to the Danites; and they turned their faces, and said to Micah, What is to thee</hi> (what is the matter), <hi type="italic">that thou hast gathered together?</hi>”
entries.1883a4f840563d959213362c428a43c0a9b1fd23: Jdg 18:24-25 <div eID="gen3475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3476" type="x-p"/> And when he replied, “<hi type="italic">Ye have taken away my gods which I made, and the priest, and have departed; what is there still to me </hi>(what have I left)? <hi type="italic">and how can ye say to me, What is to thee?</hi>” they ordered him to be silent, lest he should forfeit his life: “<hi type="italic">Let not thy voice be heard among us, lest men of savage disposition </hi>(נפשׁ מרי as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.8">2Sa 17:8</reference>) <hi type="italic">should fall upon thee</hi> (vid., Jdg 15:12; Jdg 8:21, etc.), <hi type="italic">and thou shouldst not save thy life and that of thy household,</hi>” i.e., shouldst bring death upon thyself and thy family. ואספתּה is also dependent upon פּן.
entries.3caaf1ec3dd8e05ed255b7813e484e7ce3828180: Jdg 18:26 <div eID="gen3476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3477" type="x-p"/> Then the Danites went their way; but Micah, seeing that they were stronger than he, turned back and returned home.
entries.71a5b5026ce4230c8a90677aa27ea2ea2c1129fb: Jdg 18:27-29 <div eID="gen3477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3478" type="x-p"/> And they (the Danites) had taken what Micah had made, i.e., his idols and his priest, and they fell upon Laish (על כּוא, to come over a person, to fall upon him, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.34.25">Gen 34:25</reference>), a people living quietly and free from care (vid., Jdg 18:7), smote them with the edge of the sword (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.34.26">Gen 34:26</reference>), and burned down the city (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.6.24">Jos 6:24</reference>), as it had no deliverer in its isolated condition (<hi type="italic">Jdg 18:28</hi>; cf. Jdg 18:7). It was situated “<hi type="italic">in the valley which stretches to Beth-rehob.</hi>” This valley is the upper part of the <hi type="italic">Huleh</hi> lowland, through which the central source of the Jordan (<hi type="italic">Leddan</hi>) flows, and by which <hi type="italic">Laish-Dan</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Tell el Kadi</hi>, stood (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.47">Jos 19:47</reference>). <hi type="italic">Beth-rehob</hi> is most probably the same place as the <hi type="italic">Rehob</hi> mentioned in Num 13:21, and the <hi type="italic">Beth-rehob</hi> of <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference>, which is there used to designate a part of Syria, and for which <hi type="italic">Rehob</hi> only is also used in Jdg 18:8. <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (Bibl. Res. pp. 371ff.) supposes it to be the castle of <hi type="italic">Hunin</hi> or <hi type="italic">Honin</hi>, on the south-west of Tell el Kadi; but this is hardly correct (see the remarks on Num 13:21, Pent. p. 709). The city, which lay in ashes, was afterwards rebuilt by the Danites, and called <hi type="italic">Dan</hi>, from the name of the founder of their tribe; and the ruins are still to be seen, as already affirmed, on the southern slope of the <hi type="italic">Tell el Kadi</hi> (see Rob. Bibl. Res. pp. 391-2, and the comm. on <reference osisRef="Josh.19.47">Jos 19:47</reference>).
entries.da3aeb7d64be1e5872c7189d1669cc6ca902b61a: Jdg 18:30-31 <hi type="italic">Establishment of the Image-worship in Dan</hi>. - After the rebuilding of Laish under the name of Dan, the Danites set up the pesel or image of Jehovah, which they had taken with them out of Micah’s house of God. “<hi type="italic">And Jehonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites till the day of the captivity of the land.</hi>” As the Danites had taken the Levite whom Micah had engaged for his private worship with them to Dan, and had promised him the priesthood (Jdg 18:19 and Jdg 18:27), <hi type="italic">Jehonathan</hi> can hardly be any other than this Levite. He was a son of Gershom, the son of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.22">Exo 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.18.3">Exo 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.14-1Chr.23.15">1Ch 23:14-15</reference>). Instead of בּן־משׁה, our Masoretic text has בּן־מנשּׁה with a hanging נ. With regard to this reading, the <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi> (Baba bathr.f. 109 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) observes: “Was he a son of Gershom, or was he not rather a son of Moses? as it is written, the sons of Moses were Gershom and Eliezer (<reference osisRef="1Chr.23.14">1Ch 23:14</reference>), but because he did the deeds of Manasseh (the idolatrous son of Hezekiah, 2 Kings 21) the Scripture assigns him to the family of Manasseh.” <hi type="italic">On this Rabbabar bar Channa</hi> observes, that “the prophet (i.e., the author of our book) studiously avoided calling Gershom <hi type="italic">the son of Moses</hi>, because it would have been ignominious to Moses to have had an ungodly son; but he calls him <hi type="italic">the son of Manasseh</hi>, raising the <hi type="italic">n</hi>, however, above the line, to show that it might either be inserted or omitted, and that he was the son of either מנשּׁה (Manasseh) or משׁה (Moses), - of Manasseh through imitating his impiety, of Moses by descent” (cf. <hi type="italic">Buxtorfi Tiber</hi>. p. 171). Later Rabbins say just the same. <hi type="italic">R. Tanchum</hi> calls the writing <hi type="italic">Menasseh</hi>, with a hanging <hi type="italic">nun</hi>, <hi type="italic">a</hi> סופרים תקּוּן, and speaks of <hi type="italic">ben Mosheh</hi> as <hi type="italic">Kethibh</hi>, and <hi type="italic">ben Menasseh</hi> as <hi type="italic">Keri. Ben Mosheh </hi>is therefore unquestionably the original reading, although the other reading <hi type="italic">ben Menasseh </hi>is also very old, as it is to be found in the <hi type="italic">Targums</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Syriac</hi> and <hi type="italic">Sept</hi>. versions, although some <hi type="italic">Codd</hi>. of the lxx have the reading <hi type="italic">uhiou' Moou'see'</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Kennic. dissert. gener. in V. T</hi>. §21).<note placement="foot">These two readings of the lxx seem to be fused together in the text given by <hi type="italic">Theodoret</hi> (<hi type="italic">quaest</hi>. xxvi.): Ἰωνάθαν γάρ φησίν υἱὸς Μανασσῆ, υἱοῦ Γερσὼμ υἱοῦ Μωσῆ</note><hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> also has <hi type="italic">filii Moysi</hi>. At the same time, it does not follow with certainty from the reading <hi type="italic">ben Gershom</hi> that Jehonathan was actually a son of Gershom, as <hi type="italic">ben</hi> frequently denotes a grandson in such genealogical accounts, unknown fathers being passed over in the genealogies. There is very little probability of his having been a son, for the simple reason, that if Jehonathan was the same person as Micah’s high priest - and there is no ground for doubting this - he is described as נער in Jdg 17:7; Jdg 18:3, Jdg 18:15, and therefore was at any rate a young man, whereas the son of Gershom and grandson of Moses would certainly have passed the age of youth by a few years after the death of Joshua. This Jehonathan and his sons performed the duties of the priesthood at Dan הארץ גּלות עד־יום. This statement is obscure. הארץ .eru גּלות can hardly mean anything else than the carrying away of the people of the land into exile, that is to say, of the inhabitants of Dan and the neighbourhood at least, since גּלה is the standing expression for this. Most of the commentators suppose the allusion to be to the Assyrian captivity, or primarily to the carrying away by Tiglath-Pileser of the northern tribes of Israel, viz., the population of Gilead, Galilee, and the tribe of Naphtali, in the midst of which Laish-Dan was situated (2Ki 15:29). But the statement in Jdg 18:31, “<hi type="italic">And they set them up Micah’s graven image, which he made, all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh,</hi>” is by no means reconcilable with such a conclusion. We find the house of God, i.e., the Mosaic tabernacle, which the congregation had erected at Shiloh in the days of Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>), still standing there in the time of Eli and Samuel (1Sa 1:3., Jdg 3:21; Jdg 4:3); but in the time of Saul it was at Nob (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.15">1Sa 21:1-15</reference>), and during the reign of David at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.29">1Ch 21:29</reference>). Consequently “the house of God” only stood in Shiloh till the reign of Saul, and was never taken there again. If therefore Micah’s image, which the Danites set up in Dan, remained there as long as the house of God was at Shiloh, Jonathan’s sons can only have been there till Saul’s time at the longest, and certainly cannot have been priests at this sanctuary in Dan till the time of the Assyrian captivity.<note placement="foot">The impossibility of reconciling the statement as to time in Jdg 18:31 with the idea that “the captivity of the land” refers to the Assyrian captivity, is admitted even by <hi type="italic">Bleek</hi> (Einl. p. 349), who adopts <hi type="italic">Houbigant's</hi> conjecture, viz., הארון גּלות, “the carrying away of the ark.”</note> <div eID="gen3478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3479" type="x-p"/> There are also other historical facts to be considered, which render the continuance of this Danite image-worship until the Assyrian captivity extremely improbable, or rather preclude it altogether. Even if we should not lay any stress upon the fact that the Israelites under Samuel put away the Baalim and Astartes in consequence of his appeal to them to turn to the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.4">1Sa 7:4</reference>), it is hardly credible that in the time of David the image-worship should have continued at Dan by the side of the lawful worship of Jehovah which he restored and organized, and should not have been observed and suppressed by this king, who carried on repeated wars in the northern part of his kingdom. Still more incredible would the continuance of this image-worship appear after the erection of Solomon’s temple, when all the men of Israel, and all the elders and heads of tribes, came to Jerusalem, at the summons of Solomon, to celebrate the consecration of this splendid national sanctuary (1 Kings 5-7). Lastly, the supposition that the image-worship established by the Danites at Dan still continued to exist, is thoroughly irreconcilable with the fact, that when Jeroboam established the kingdom of the ten tribes he had two golden calves made as images of Jehovah for the subjects of his kingdom, and set up one of them at Dan, and appointed priests out of the whole nation who were not of the sons of Levi. If an image-worship of Jehovah had been still in existence in Dan, and conducted by Levitical priests. Jeroboam would certainly not have established a second worship of the same kind under priests who were not Levitical. All these difficulties preclude our explaining the expression, “the day of the captivity of the land,” as referring to either the Assyrian or Babylonian captivity. It can only refer to some event which took place in the last years of Samuel, or the first part of the reign of Saul. David Kimchi and many others have interpreted the expression as relating to the carrying away of the ark by the Philistines, for which the words מיּשׂראל כבוד גּלה are used in <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.21-1Sam.4.22">1Sa 4:21-22</reference> (e.g., <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>, Beitr. vol. ii. pp. 153ff.; Hävernick, Einl. ii. 1, p. 109; <hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>, and others). With the carrying away of the ark of the covenant, the tabernacle lost its significance as a sanctuary of Jehovah. We learn from <reference osisRef="Ps.78.59-Ps.78.64">Psa 78:59-64</reference> how the godly in Israel regarded that event. They not only looked upon it as a casting away of the dwelling-lace of God at Shiloh; but in the fact that Jehovah gave up His might and glory (i.e., the ark) into captivity, they discerned a surrender of the nation into the full power of its foes which resembled a carrying away into captivity. For, apart altogether form the description in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.62-Ps.78.64">Psa 78:62-64</reference>, we may infer with certainty from the account of the tyranny which these foes still exercised over the Israelites in the time of Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.19-1Sam.13.23">1Sa 13:19-23</reference>), that, after this victory, the Philistines may have completely subjugated the Israelites, and treated them as their prisoners. We may therefore affirm with <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>, that “the author looked upon the whole land as carried away into captivity in its sanctuary, which formed as it were its kernel and essence.” If, however, this figurative explanation of הארץ גּלות should not be accepted, there is no valid objection to our concluding that the words refer to some event with which we have no further acquaintance, in which the city of Dan was conquered by the neighbouring Syrians, and the inhabitants carried away into captivity. For it is evident enough from the fact of the kings of <hi type="italic">Zoba</hi> being mentioned, in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, among the different enemies of Israel against whom Saul carried on war, that the Syrians also invaded Israel in the tie of the Philistine supremacy, and carried Israelites away out of the conquered towns and districts. The Danite image-worship, however, was probably suppressed and abolished when Samuel purified the land and people from idolatry, after the ark had been brought back by the Philistines (1 Sam. 2 ff.).  <chapter eID="Judg.18"/> <div eID="gen3479" type="x-p"/>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In one of these Houses, the Plural number for the Singular, as <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 12. 7.</ns0:note> an ephod, and teraphim, and a graven image, and a molten image? Now therefore consider what ye have to do <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther it be not expedient; either, 1. To consult them again for your own satisfaction; or, rather, 2. To take them away for your further use, as you shall have oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion; for their action is the best Comment upon their words.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And they turned thitherward, and came to the house of the young man the Levite, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the house of Micah, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> ask<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> him of pe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> saluted him<ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>asked him of Peace, i. e.</ns0:hi> if he were in peace, <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> being commonly put for Health and Prospe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And the six hundred men appointed with their weapons of war, which <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> of the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of Dan, stood by the entring of the gate.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the five men that went to spy out the land went up, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> came in thither <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, into the House, and that part of it, where those things were.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> took the graven image, and the ephod, and the tera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phim, and the molten image, and the priest stood in the entring of the gate<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Whither they had drawn him forth, that they might without noise or hindrance take them away.</ns0:note> with the six hundred men <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> appointed with weapons of war.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And these <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, the five mentioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17.</ns0:note> went into Micahs house: and fetched the carved image, the ephod, and the te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raphim, and the molten image; then said the priest unto them, What do ye<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">What do you mean to do? I hope you will not do so Impious and Injurious an action.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And they said unto him, Hold thy peace, lay thy hand upon thy mouth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Be silent, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 21. 5. and 29. 9. and 40. 4. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30. 32. The same thing repeated in other words.</ns0:note>, and go with us, and be to us a father, and a priest<ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">See on <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 17. 10.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>Is it</ns0:hi> better for thee to be a priest unto the house of one man, or that thou be a priest unto a tribe, and a family <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:hi>a tribe, that is, (and</ns0:hi> being oft put for <ns0:hi>that is) a family.</ns0:hi> For it is certain this was not an expedition of the whole tribe, which num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bred 64000 men, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 26. 43. but only of one family, which it seems were more vexed with the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Amorites,</ns0:hi> and therefore resolved to seek new habitations at a great distance from them. And after this time we find the Body of the <ns0:hi>Danites</ns0:hi> in their old and proper portions in <ns0:hi>Sampson's</ns0:hi> time, which, though placed before this, was long after it.</ns0:note> in Israel?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And the priests heart was glad <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Being wholly governed by his own Interest, and making all his obligations of Justice and Gratitude give place to it. But it is not strange, if he who was before perfidious to God, should prove so to men.</ns0:note>, and he took the ephod, and the teraphim, and the graven image, and went in the midst of the people <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Among the People: or properly in the midst, both for the greater security of such precious things, and that <ns0:hi>Micah</ns0:hi> might not be able to come at him, either to injure or upbraid him; and, it may be, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause that was the place where the Ark used to be carried.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 So they turned and departed, and put the little ones, and the cattel, and the carriage before them <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For their greater security, if <ns0:hi>Micah</ns0:hi> should pursue them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 ¶ <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> when they were a good way from the house of Micah, the men <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> in the houses near to Micahs house, were gathered together, and overtook the children of Dan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And they cried unto the children of Dan: and they turned their faces, and said unto Micah, What ails thee, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> that thou art ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thered toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:note> that thou comest with such a company?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And he said, Ye have taken away my gods
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:208" />
which I made <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">So far was he besotted with Superstition and Idolatry, that he esteemed those gods, which were man's work. But he could not be so stupid, as to think these were indeed the great <ns0:hi>Iehovah</ns0:hi> that made Heaven and Earth; but only a lower sort of gods, by whom, as Mediators, he offered up his Wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship unto the true God, as it is manifest divers of the Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thens did.</ns0:note>, and the priest, and ye are gone away: and what have I more<ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I value nothing I have in comparison of what you have taken away. Which zeal for Idolatrous trash may shame multitudes that call themselves Christians, and yet ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parently value their Worldly conveniences more than all the concerns even of the true Religion, and of their own Salvation.</ns0:note>? and what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> ye say unto me, What aileth thee?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 ¶ And the children of Dan said unto him, Let not thy voice <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The complaints and reproaches.</ns0:note> be heard among us: lest <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Hebr.</ns0:hi> bitter of soul.</ns0:note> angry fellows <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Soldiers, who are in themselves sharp and fierce, and will soon be enflamed by thy provoking words.</ns0:note> run upon thee, and thou lose thy life <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which, notwithstanding all thy pretences, thou dost value more than thy Images, as indeed appeared from his following practice.</ns0:note>, with the lives of thy houshold.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And the children of Dan went their way: and when Micah saw that they <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> too strong for him, he turned, and went back unto his house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And they took <ns0:hi>the things</ns0:hi> which Micah had made, and the priest which he had, and came unto Laish, unto a people <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> at quiet, and secure, and they smote them with the edge of the sword, and burnt the city with fire <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not wholly, but in a great measure, to strike the greater terror into the Inhabitants, and to make their conquest of the place more easie.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> no deliverer, because it <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> far from Zidon, and they had no business with <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> man: and it <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in the valley that <ns0:hi>lieth</ns0:hi> by Beth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rehob <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">A place near <ns0:hi>Libanus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hamath:</ns0:hi> of which see <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 13. 21. <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 19. 28. and 21. 31. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 1. 31.</ns0:note>, and they built a city, and dwelt therein.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And they called the name of the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>osh. 19. 47.</ns0:note> city Dan, after the name of Dan their Father <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That it might be manifest, that they belonged to the tribe of <ns0:hi>Dan,</ns0:hi> though they were seated at a great distance from them, even in the most-Northerly part of the Land: whereas the lot of their tribe was in the Southern part of <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, who was born unto Israel: howbeit, the name of the city was Laish at the first.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 ¶ And the children of Dan set them up the graven image<ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Having succeeded in their expedition according to the prediction which, as they supposed, they had from this Image, they had a great veneration for it.</ns0:note>: and Jonathan the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he, and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan, until the day of the captivity of the land<ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either 1. When the <ns0:hi>Ark</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were taken captives by the <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 4. 10, 11. Though there is no mention of any who were then taken captives, or that the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> did pursue the Victory, and Conquer the Land at that time, for their Victory was quickly damped, and turned to Mourn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 5. Or 2. After that time, when the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> slew <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ionathan,</ns0:hi> and discomfited the whole Host of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and made the rest of the People flee out of their Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties, and took possession of their Cities and Land. Or 3. When the whole Land of the ten Tribes, whereof <ns0:hi>Dan</ns0:hi> was one, was Conquered, and the People carried Captive by the <ns0:hi>Assyrian,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 17. 6, 23. which is called by way of Emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nency, <ns0:hi>the Captivity,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 5. 22. But against this it is Objected, That it is not probable, that this Idolatry should continue so long in such a publick place and manner: or that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> would suffer it. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> It is not said, that the <ns0:hi>graven Image</ns0:hi> was there so long, for that is restrained to a shorter date, even to the continuance of the Ark in <ns0:hi>Shiloh, v.</ns0:hi> 31. which was removed thence, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 4. But only that <ns0:hi>Ionathan's</ns0:hi> posterity were Priests to this Tribe or Family of <ns0:hi>Dan,</ns0:hi> which they might be under all the changes, even till the <ns0:hi>Assyrian</ns0:hi> Captivity, sometimes more openly and allowedly, sometimes more cunningly, sometimes more se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cretly, sometimes in one way of Superstition or Idolatry, and sometimes in another; and, in and after <ns0:hi>Ieroboam's</ns0:hi> time, in the Worship of the Calves, for which service though he did make Priests of the meanest of the People, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 12. 31. yet that was not by choice, but out of necessity, because the Priests and <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> generally forsook him, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 11. 13, 14. and therefore when he could engage any of the Priests or <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> in that service, he was doubtless very glad of them to gain reputation to his Impious and absurd device.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And they set them up Micah's graven image, which he made, all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh.</ns0:p>
